subject: Basic lasso regression—penalization does not occur!

messages.author: 7565f5fa3c6e8fc3
messages.subject: Basic lasso regression—penalization does not occur!
parts:
I'm trying to implement basic l1 penalization in a regression formula, but have been having no luck at all.

I've attached three files:
  • lm-lasso-comparison.R compares frequentist estimates to Bayesian estimates
  • lm.stan implements a linear regression
  • lasso.stan is intended to impose a lasso penalty on the coefficients in lm.stan
Specifically, in lasso.stan, I've adapted the code from page 360 of the manual for stan 2.14.0, but when I run the code, I get the following output:
> fitted_summary
                    lm   stan_lm      lasso stan_lasso
(Intercept)  2.2491402 2.2431029 5.46908324  2.2853728
Petal.Length 0.4719200 0.4720354 0.09958757  0.4704120
Sepal.Width  0.5955247 0.5974505 0.00000000  0.5858015

These are posterior means, rather than the mode, and I understand the posterior mean is not an appropriate point estimate when applying a Bayesian lasso.

But, the estimates returned by lm.stan and lasso.stan appear identical (to me), and the penalty term seems to have no effect! I get similarly perplexing results from the variable opt_lasso...

I have also tried modeling the regression coefficients with a Laplace / double exponential prior, to no avail.

I suspect this is a stupid mistake, but I'm just not seeing it. Can anyone offer any suggestions?

Thanks for any help you can offer!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Basic lasso regression—penalization does not occur!
parts:
All this terminology is terribly confused in the literature.

The "lasso" usually refers to penalized maximum likelihood estimates
with L1 penalties. You have to choose the scale of that penalty.
Thus "Bayesian lasso" is an oxymoron.

You can include a Laplace prior in a Bayesian model, and then
the posterior is proportional to the penalized likelihood, so if
you take the mode (the so-called MAP estimate), it's just the
Lasso again. But there's nothing Bayesian about MAP estimates.

The posterior mean (or median) is a Bayesian estimator (in that
it's calculated with an expectation over the posterior). But we
know posterior means and posterior modes can be quite distant in
models with asymmetric posteriors.

Stan provides penalized maximum likelihood. Unlike specialized
lasso software, it's unlikely to find estimates of exactly zero for
parameters. The Bayesian posterior means are never going to be zero
(the event of parameter being equal to zero has probability zero).

Otherwise, your code's OK, though comparing to other software, you
need to make sure that you're dealing with lambdas on the same scale.

Also, this

for (j in 1:p)
target += - lambda * fabs(beta[p]);

can be coded as

target += -lambda * sum(fabs(beta));

or as

beta ~ double_exponential(0, ?);

where you need to figure out what the scale is to match whatever
the Lasso people do.

The absolute value (same as in Laplace prior) is bad news in that it
means the posterior isn't continuously differentiable. Stan's samplers
and optimizers can run into problems when the parameter jumps across
that non-differentiable point.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Basic lasso regression—penalization does not occur!
parts:
On Monday, February 13, 2017 at 3:58:09 PM UTC-5, michaer...@gmail.com wrote:
Thanks for your response! Your points on Bayesian treatments of lasso are much appreciated, and as far as my question RE comparisons with other software, you were right on the money—I forgot to standardize.

FYI, in the rstanarm package we have the stan_lm(), which is sort of like ridge regression, and stan_glm() with family = gaussian and prior = laplace() or prior = lasso(). The latter estimates the shrinkage as a hyperparameter while the former fixes it to a specified value. Again, there are possible differences in scaling but you should get good predictions. Also, there is prior = hs() or prior = hs_plus() that implement hierarchical shrinkage on the coefficients.

Ben
